analytic.title: Improving Schedulability and Energy Performance for Weakly Hard Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: For real-time embedded systems, schedulability and energy efficiency are two highly co-related important design issues. In this paper, we explore how to improve the schedulability and energy efficiency for real-time systems with weakly hard temporal constraints. The weakly hard temporal constraints are modeled by the (m, k)-constraints, which require that at least m out of any k consecutive jobs of a task meet their deadlines. Two off-line approaches are proposed for managing the appropriate mandatory/optional job partition for a given task set with (m, k)-constraints. Through extensive experiments, the results demonstrate that our proposed techniques significantly outperform previous approaches in both schedulability and energy performance for weakly hard real-time embedded systems.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In traditional hard real-time embedded systems, all task instances are required to meet their deadlines and any deadline miss will crash the entire application or system. However, few real-time applications are truly hard real-time. For example, many real-time applications, such as multimedia processing and real-time communication systems, can often tolerate occasional deadline misses. Some other applications may have soft deadlines where tasks that do not finish by their deadlines can still be completed with a reduced value [1] or they can simply be dropped provided that the user's perceived quality of service (QoS) is satisfied. To quantify the QoS requirements, some statistic information such as the average deadline miss rate is commonly used. Although the statistical deadline miss rate can ensure the quality of service in a probabilistic manner, this metric can be problematic for some real-time applications. For example, for certain real-time systems, when some tasks miss their deadlines, the information carried by those tasks can be estimated with reasonable accuracy using techniques such as interpolation. However, even a very low overall miss rate tolerance cannot prevent a large number of deadline misses from occurring in such a short period of time that the data cannot be successfully reconstructed. To avoid possible severe consequences, one can always treat the system as a hard realtime system. The problem, however, is that when the system is overloaded 1 , the approaches for hard real-time systems are no longer valid as deadline missing will become inevitable in such kind of scenarios. As a result, critical information that cannot be reconstructed may be lost, thus the service quality can be severely degraded from the user's perspective.

The concept of weakly hard real-time system is more suitable for modeling such kind of applications. In the weakly hard real-time model, the system should not only support the overall guarantee of the QoS statistically, but also be able to provide a lower bounded, predictable level of QoS in each specified time interval. The (m, k)-model, proposed by Hamdaoui et al. [2], can serve well for this purpose. According to this model, a repetitive task of the system is associated with an (m, k)(0 < m ≤ k) constraint requiring that m out of any k consecutive job instances of the task meet their deadlines. A dynamic failure occurs, which implies that the temporal QoS constraint is violated and the scheduler is thus considered having failed, if within any k consecutive jobs less than m job instances meet their deadlines. Based on this (m, k)-model, Ramanathan et al. [3] proposed to partition the jobs into mandatory and optional jobs. So long as all the mandatory jobs can meet their deadlines, the (m, k)-constraints can be ensured. West et al. [4] introduced another model, called the window-constrained model, which requires that at least m jobs over any non-overlapped and consecutive windows containing k jobs meet their deadlines. It can be readily concluded that window constraints are weaker than the (m, k)-constraints, as if a schedule is feasible under the (m, k)-constraints, it is also feasible under the window constraints.

For real-time embedded systems, energy minimization has also come to be recognized as one of the primary design goals. Dynamic voltage/frequency scaling (DVFS), e.g. [5], which dynamically varies the supply voltage and frequency of the processing unit, has proven to be an effective way to reduce energy consumption. Moreover, since energy consumption is a convex function of the processor speed, which is proportional to the supply voltage [6], the energy efficiency of embedded systems is closely related to the schedulability of the system. In other words, if the schedulability of the task sets can be improved, the running speeds of the processor to execute the jobs can be lowered correspondingly and thus the energy consumption can be reduced.

In this paper, we study the feasibility issues for weakly hard real-time systems. Specifically, we will explore how to improve the schedulability and energy efficiency for such kind of systems through more adaptive mandatory/optional job partitioning while ensuring the (m, k)-guarantee. Since compared to the fixed-priority scheme, the earliest deadline first (EDF) scheme allows the task set to be executed under higher CPU utilizations and thus has better potential for improving energy efficiency through voltage scaling, we assume that the realtime tasks are scheduled according to the EDF scheduling policy.

Two approaches are proposed in this paper for determining the appropriate mandatory/optional job partition for a given task set. In the first approach, the mandatory job sets of each task for the given systems are evenly distributed, which is based on enhancing the previous work proposed in [3]. Due to the inherent properties of some real world applications (for example, the task periods of some practical systems are often close to harmonic), strictly evenly distributed patterns might not always yield good results for the purpose of improving schedulability and energy efficiency. To take into account these scenarios, we also propose a second approach in which the mandatory jobs are determined more adaptively based on the simulated annealing (SA) algorithm. Through our extensive experiments, the results show that our proposed approaches can significantly improve simultaneously the schedulability and energy efficiency for weakly hard real-time systems .

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces related work. Section III presents the system models and motivations. Section IV introduces our first approach in enhancing the previous mandatory/optional job partition approaches based on evenly distributed patterns. Section V introduces our second approach which is able to find more general mandatory/optional job partition patterns based on a simulated annealing algorithm. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated using experimental results in section VI. In section VII, we offer some conclusions.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Due to its intuitiveness and capability of capturing not only statistical but also deterministic QoS requirements, the (m, k)model has been widely studied, e.g., [7], [2], [3]. In [7], Quan et al. formally proved that the problem of scheduling with (m, k)-guarantee for arbitrary values of m and k is NPhard in the strong sense. To guarantee the (m, k)-constraints, Ramanathan et al. [3] proposed a strategy to partition the jobs into mandatory and optional jobs. The mandatory jobs are the jobs that must meet their deadlines in order to satisfy the (m, k)-constraints, while the optional jobs can be executed to further improve the quality of the service or simply be dropped to save computing resources.

In [7], Quan et al. improved the above partitioning strategy by reducing the maximal interference from high priority mandatory jobs to lower priority mandatory jobs. However, since the "interference" is computed for task sets based on fixed-priority assignment, it is not applicable when the system is scheduled under the EDF scheduling policy. In [7], a genetic algorithm (GA) was also introduced to find a more general partitioning strategy for task sets scheduled using fixed-priority scheduling. For the same reason it cannot be applied to task sets scheduled under the EDF scheduling policy, either. Another limitation of their GA algorithm is that for a task set which is already underloaded (therefore schedulable with any pattern), their approach did not consider the pattern assignment that can minimize the energy consumption of the system, while in this paper we will propose a simulated-annealing-based approach to solve this problem.

In [8], Bernat et al. proposed using a Bi-Modal scheduler to schedule the systems with (m, k)-constraints. The tasks are first scheduled according to the generic scheduling policy in the normal mode, and switched to panic mode if the dynamic failure is likely to occur. This work also targets systems with fixed-priority assignment. Note that none of the works above has taken energy/power consumption into consideration. Some other studies [9], [10], [11], [12] have also been conducted related to reducing energy consumption for real-time systems with QoS constraints based on mandatory/optional job partitioning strategies. However, the application of all these approaches are limited to systems that are already schedulable under certain known mandatory/optional job partitioning strategies such as the deeply-red pattern [13] or the evenly distributed pattern [3]. Otherwise the (m, k)-constraints cannot be guaranteed in the worst case. As will be shown in Section III-C and Section VI-A in this paper, the deeply-red pattern [13] and the evenly distributed pattern [3] can only account for a limited category of feasible partitioning strategies and there still exists quite a number of mandatory/optional job partitions which are schedulable but cannot be effectively handled by these known partitioning strategies. On the other hand, with energy consumption being an increasingly important concern in real-time embedded systems design, very few studies have been reported in enhancing the energy conservation by searching for better patterns to improve the mandatory/optional job partitioning of the whole system directly. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to combine these two important issues and simultaneously improve the schedulability and energy efficiency for weakly hard real-time systems .

div.head: III. PRELIMINARIES
div.p: In this section, we first introduce the system and energy model as well as the problem definitions. Then we present the motivations for our research.

div.head: A. System model
div.p: The real-time system considered in this paper contains n independent periodic tasks, T = {τ 0 , τ 1 , ⋅⋅⋅, τ n-1 }, scheduled according to the earliest deadline first (EDF) policy [14]. Each task contains an infinite sequence of periodically arriving instances called jobs. Task τ i is characterized using five parameters, i.e., (P i , D i , C i , m i , k i ). P i , D i (D i ≤ P i ), and C i denote the period, the deadline and the worst case execution time for τ i , respectively. A pair of integers, i.e., (m i , k i ) (0 < m i ≤ k i ), denote the QoS requirement for τ i , requiring that, among any consecutive k i jobs of τ i , at least m i jobs must meet their deadlines. The l th job of task τ i is denoted as J il and its arrival time and absolute deadline are denoted as r il and d il .

div.head: B. Energy model
div.p: The real time task sets can be executed on a DVFS processor that can operate at a finite set of discrete supply voltage levels V = {V 1 , ...,V max }, each with an associated speed s i which is normalized to the processor speed at V max .

The power consumption of the DVFS processor can be divided into two parts: the speed-dependent part P dep (s) and the speed-independent part P ind . The speed-dependent power consumption P dep (s) mainly comes from the dynamic power consumption and short-circuit power consumption, while the speed-independent power consumption mainly comes from the leakage. The dynamic power mainly consists of the switching power for charging and discharging the load capacitance and can be represented [6] as P dyn = C L V 2 f , where C L is the load capacitance, V is the supply voltage, and f is the system clock frequency. The leakage power is mainly due to the subthreshold leakage current and the reverse bias junction current in the CMOS circuit. If the leakage power consumption is related to the speeds/voltages, it can be divided into two parts that contribute to P dep (s) and P ind accordingly. So the total power consumption when the processor is in its active status, i.e, P act (s), is thus P act(s) = P dep (s) + P ind . The speed dependant power P dep (s) can be modeled as a strictly convex and increasing function of s. It can usually be expressed as P dep (s) = αs m , where m is a constant between 2 and 3 [15].

The processor can be in one of the three states: active, idle and sleeping states. When the processor is idle, the major portion of the power consumption comes from the leakage which increases rapidly. Shutting-down strategy, i.e., putting the processor into its sleeping state, can greatly reduce the leakage energy. However, it has to pay extra energy and timing overhead to shut down and later wake up the processor. Assume that the power consumptions of a processor in its idle state and sleeping state are P idle and P sleep , respectively, and the energy overhead and the timing overhead of shutdown/wakeup is E o and t o . Then the processor can be shut down with positive energy gains only when the length of the idle interval is larger than T th = max( E o P idle -P sleep ,t o ). We call T th the shut down threshold interval.

When the processor is active, without considering the leakage, it would be most energy efficient to run the tasks with supply voltage as low as possible. However, reducing the supply voltage usually requires the reduction of the threshold voltage to maintain the circuit performance, which will dramatically increase the leakage current and, hence, the leakage power consumption. Considering a job with workload w and total power function P act (s), the total energy (E act (s)) consumed to finish this job with speed s can be represented as E act (s) = P act (s) × w s . Hence, to minimize E act (s), let ∂E act (s) ∂s = 0. When

div.head: C. Problem definitions and motivations
div.p: With the above system models, the problems to be explored in this paper can be stated as follows:
div.formula: Problem 1: Given system T = {τ 0 , τ 1 , ⋅⋅⋅, τ n-1 }, τ i = (P i , D i , C i , m i , k i ), i = 0, ⋅⋅⋅, (n-1), schedule T with EDF such that all (m, k)-constraints are satisfied. Problem 2: Given system T = {τ 0 , τ 1 , ⋅⋅⋅, τ n-1 }, τ i = (P i , D i , C i , m i , k i ), i = 0, ⋅⋅⋅, (n-1)
div.p: , schedule T with EDF on a variable voltage processor with limited supply voltage levels such that all (m, k)-constraints are satisfied and the energy consumption is minimized.
Obviously Problem 1 and Problem 2 are co-dependent and the solution for Problem 1 will be very useful in solving Problem 2.
In what follows, we will introduce some concepts as well as the motivations related to these problems.

To solve the above problems, a key problem is to judiciously partition the jobs into mandatory jobs and optional jobs [7] and schedule them most efficiently. For ease of explanation, we adopt the concept of (m, k)-pattern as introduced in [7].

It is not hard to see that the mandatory job set assigned according to the E-pattern or the E R -pattern has better schedulability than that by the R-pattern due to its even distribution of mandatory jobs within each task [9]. However, even though the mandatory jobs for each task are evenly distributed, the overall Even though it is shown [9] that the E-pattern (or E Rpattern) has very good schedulability compared with other (m, k)-patterns when all (k i × P i )'s are (or close to) co-prime with each other, in practical applications, the task periods often contain some large common divisors (e.g., CNC (Computerized Numerical Control) machine controller [16], Avionics, and INS (Inertial Navigation System) [17], etc.). The E-pattern (or E R -pattern) is not necessarily the best candidate in this scenario. Moreover, it is proven in [7] that to find the optimal (m, k)-patterns for the general case is NP-hard in the strong sense. In this paper, we will explore how to determine the appropriate (m, k)-patterns for a given task set. Our approaches are based on the following definitions and observations:

Moreover, to check the schedulability of the system, we have the following lemma:
div.formula: Lemma 1: Given system T = {τ 0 , τ 1 , ⋅⋅⋅, τ n-1 } with τ i = (P i , D i ,C i , m i , k i ) to be scheduled with EDF under a given (m, k)-pattern, T is schedulable if the intensity of the highest- intensity interval, i.e., I(t H s ,t H f )
div.p: , is less than or equal to 1. Proof: If we assume the maximal normalized processor speed to be 1, the result follows the conclusions in [5].

Note that given a task set with an arbitrary (m, k)-constraint, to check its feasibility is NP-hard for the general case [7] and the usual way is to resort to simulation to check in each case whether each mandatory job can be finished before its deadline. However, with Lemma 1, in each case it is sufficient to just inspect whether the intensity I(t H s ,t H f ) of the highestintensity interval is greater than 1 or not. Since I(t H s ,t H f ) can be computed in O(Nlog 2 N) time, it also provides us with a more efficient way to check the schedulability for a given task set under each particular (m, k)-pattern.

As seen in the motivation example in Figure 1, by distributing the mandatory workload of the whole task set more evenly, the schedulability of the task set could be improved. Moreover, with energy consumption as a convex function of the job speed [6] we could expect to reduce the energy consumption of the whole system effectively if the mandatory workload of the whole task set can be distributed more evenly. In order to do so, we should try to determine the (m, k)-pattern appropriately such that the difference between the intensities of the highest/lowest-intensity intervals is reduced as much as possible. Obviously to achieve this goal, one effective way is to determine the (m, k)-pattern in such a way that the maximum intensity I(t H s ,t H f ) of the system is minimized. In what follows, we formulate this issue as a programming problem. Specifically, given a system T , our goal is to find the appropriate regular (m, k)-pattern for each task τ i such that the corresponding I(t H s ,t H f ) of the task set is minimized. The latter one has been proven to be NP-hard in the strong sense [7]. However, it does give us some hints in searching for the appropriate (m, k)-pattern based on some existing results. From Lemma 1, it is not hard to see that the feasibility of the task set depends on the maximum intensity of the system, i.e., I(t H s ,t H f ). Therefore if the value of I(t H s ,t H f ) can be reduced, the schedulability of the task set can be improved correspondingly.

For the existing (m, k)-patterns, i.e., E-pattern, E R -pattern, and R-pattern, we know that the schedulabilities of the Epattern and E R -pattern are much better than the R-pattern [9]. However, from the motivation example in Fig 1, we saw that the E-pattern or E R -pattern is not always desirable. div.head: IV. ENHANCING THE EVENLY DISTRIBUTED PATTERN
div.p: The problem of the E-pattern is that although the mandatory jobs for each task are evenly distributed, the overall mandatory workload for the whole task set is not necessarily evenly distributed (a similar problem is also observed for the E Rpattern). For example, under the E-pattern, the first job of each task is always designated as mandatory and overlaps with the first job of other tasks at the starting time. As a result, the maximal intensity I(t H s ,t H f ) of the task set might be higher than it could be, which would affect the schedulability of the task set adversely. In order to improve the schedulability, one way is to vary the E-pattern appropriately to reduce I(t H s ,t H f ) of the resulting task set. In [7], Quan et al. proposed an approach to vary the E-pattern partitioning strategy by reducing the maximal mandatory interference from higher priority tasks on lower priority tasks. However, since the interference is computed using fixed-priority scheduling (as mentioned in Section II), it is not applicable to task sets scheduled under EDF. In this section, we will explore how to vary the E-pattern properly to improve the schedulability for task sets scheduled under EDF.

From our objective function in Equation ( 4), we can see that to improve the schedulability of the task set, the main problem is how to reduce its maximal intensity I(t H s ,t H f ). In the following, we will try to solve this problem by redistributing the mandatory workload among different tasks. Before that, we first introduce the following definition:

Definition 5: (Critical mandatory workload point) The critical mandatory workload point of τ i ( denoted as CMT i ) under the E-pattern is defined to be the time point which has a maximal number of consecutive mandatory jobs of τ i .

It is not hard to see that for the E-pattern time 0 is the first critical mandatory workload point CMT i for each task τ i . Moreover, according to the properties of the regular (m, k)pattern, CMT i is a periodic event with period k i P i and with initial time O i = 0.

div.head: V. FROM EVENLY DISTRIBUTED PATTERN TO GENERAL REGULAR PATTERN ASSIGNMENT -A SIMULATED ANNEALING APPROACH
div.p: Although the approach in Algorithm 1 can improve the schedulability of evenly distributed patterns, there still exists a large number of task sets that cannot be scheduled with any kind of evenly distributed pattern. For example, for the task set in Figure 2(a), regardless of how we rotate the evenly distributed patterns as in Figure 2(b) and (c), the task set cannot be schedulable, while other non-evenly distributed regular patterns such as the one in Figure 2(d) can be well schedulable. Since it is a NP-hard problem to find the optimal regular pattern for the general case, to schedule such kind of task sets, more advanced techniques are desired. In [7], Quan et. al introduced a genetic algorithm to find the general regular (m, k)-pattern (not necessarily evenly distributed) for task sets based on fixed-priority scheduling. Compared with the approach in [7], our objective function in Equation ( 4) is more suitable for solving such kind of problems under EDF. Based on it, we will introduce a heuristic, which is based on the Simulated Annealing (SA) algorithm, to solve the problem of finding a general regular (m, k)-pattern.

Simulated Annealing (SA) is a generic probabilistic metaheuristic for the global optimization problem. The technique has been applied to a variety of problems in real-time scheduling such as task allocation and priority assignment [19]. The SA method models the physical process of heating a material and then slowly lowering the temperature to decrease defects, thus minimizing the system energy. Contrary to the local search methods, the SA algorithm allows the solution to escape from a local minimum, but not a global one.

In the general SA algorithm, first an initial solution is randomly generated and used as the starting point. Then the cost/energy at this point is evaluated. The objective of the algorithm is to minimize the final cost/energy. To continue, an iterative loop is performed. During each iteration a neighbor solution is chosen randomly and its cost/energy is evaluated. If the neighbor solution is better than the initial solution, then it is accepted as the new initial solution. Otherwise, the neighbor solution is accepted only with a probability which decreases exponentially with the cost/energy difference and is slowly lowered with time. According to [20], the probability can be defined as min(1, e -Δ T ), where Δ is the difference of the cost/energy between the initial solution and the new solution and T is the control parameter corresponding to the temperature of the physical analogy. By repeating the above iterations (until some stopping criterion is met) while slowly lowering the temperature, the algorithm eventually converges to the global optimum.

In an SA algorithm, it is important to select the initial configuration as it will affect both the quality of the solution and also the computation time. In our approach, instead of choosing the initial solution randomly, we use the (m, k)pattern that is output by Algorithm 1 as the starting point. Then during each loop, by iteratively improving the initial (m, k)-pattern based on its cost/energy evaluation with the objective function in Equation ( 4), we can expect to eventually find the most appropriate regular (m, k)-pattern that can minimize the objective function (4). The salient part of our SA approach is presented in Algorithm 2.

Randomly generate a number R ∈ [0, 1]; As shown in Algorithm 2, our approach firstly takes the task set with an (m, k)-pattern generated by Algorithm 1 as the input. Then based on it the highest/lowest-intensity intervals, i.e., [t H s , tH f ]/[t L s , tL f ] of the task set are computed with Yao's algorithm. Each neighbor solution is obtained by randomly picking out one task τ i and changing one of the mandatory jobs in its (m, k)-pattern to optional. Meanwhile, to satisfy the (m, k)-constraint, we should also promote one optional job in its (m, k)-pattern to mandatory. After that, we update the repeated regular (m, k)-pattern for τ i and recompute the highest/lowest-intensity intervals for the whole task set, i.e.,
div.formula: [ t′ H s , t′ H f ]/[ t′ L s , t′ L f ]
div.p: of the new solution. The modification is accepted only if the maximal intensity I( t′ H s , t′ H f ) of the new solution is less than that of the initial solution (line 9-10) or with a probability which decreases exponentially with their intensity difference and is lowered in each iteration (line [13][14][15][16][17][18]. The algorithm terminates when the stop criterion is met (line 21), i.e., when the maximal intensity I( t′ H s , t′ H f ) of the new solution has been frozen and has stopped decreasing in the last few temperatures or the temperature has been reduced to zero.

The complexity of the SA approach in Algorithm 2 mainly comes from the loop in which Yao's algorithm is used to compute the the highest/lowest-intensity intervals. With a proper segment tree data structure, Yao's algorithm can be implemented in O(Nlog 2 N) time [5], where N is the number of jobs within the hyperperiod. So the total time complexity of Algorithm 2 is O(kNlog 2 N). Here k is the number of loops to be performed, which is determined by the initial temperature and the cooling rate. Note that, SA is inherently sequential and hence very slow for problems with large search spaces. In [21], advanced exploration algorithms based on Markov Decision Process were proposed to minimize the number of necessary evaluations. Although similar approaches can be applied to our work to speed up the search process of SA, here we opt to narrow the search space by exploiting the domain knowledge provided by the highest/lowest-intensity intervals, i.e.,
div.formula: [ t′ H s , t′ H f ]/ [ t′ L s , t′ L f ],
div.p: which is much easier to implement. Specifically, in selecting the task to switch its mandatory/optional job patterns within its (m, k)-pattern, we try to select a task that has mandatory/optional jobs as close to
div.formula: [ t′ H s , t′ H f ]/[ t′ L s , t′ L f ] as possible (line 6
div.p: ). The priority is given to the task with both mandatory and optional jobs completely falling within [ t′ H s , t′ H f ] and [ t′ L s , t′ L f ] simultaneously. By switching the mandatory/optional job patterns of such kind of task within its (m, k)-pattern, we could expect to make the mandatory workload within the hyper period be distributed more evenly from the perspective of the whole task set.

In SA algorithm, the efficiency of the algorithm also depends on the initial temperature and the cooling rate. In our algorithm, we determined the initial temperature based on the maximal intensity difference ΔI 0 between the highest and lowest-intensity intervals of the initial solution and the acceptance probability under the initial temperature, i.e., set Init Temperature = -ΔI 0 ln α , where α is the value of the cooling factor, which is a value between (0, 1) and should be determined empirically to give good results. In particular, in our approach, the cooling factor is set to be 0.95 to generate results with good quality and within acceptable time cost. An example As an example to show how our SA algorithm works, consider the same task set in Figure 2(a). The pattern output by Algorithm 1 is shown in Figure 2(c) and taken as input. Based on it, our SA algorithm works as follows:

First, the highest and lowest-intensity intervals in the configuration of Figure 2(c) are computed with Yao's algorithm, which are [0,12] and [16,20] with corresponding intensities as 7 6 and 0, respectively. The initial temperature was set to be Init Temperature = -( 76 -0) ln 0.95 = 22.75. Then during the first iteration, we try to select the tasks with mandatory and optional jobs completely falling within [0,12] and [16,20] simultaneously to switch its mandatory/optional job pattern 1.17 0.75 1.17

1.17 correspondingly. For this particular configuration only task τ 1 is qualified (in case there are multiple such kind of tasks, we just randomly pick one of them). After the mandatory and optional job patterns of τ 1 within [0,12] and [16,20] are switched correspondingly as shown in Figure 3(a), we recompute the highest and lowest-intensity intervals of the current configuration with Yao's algorithm, which are [0,12] and [12,24] with corresponding intensities as 11 12 = 0.92 and 3 4 = 0.75, respectively. After that, we evaluate the new configuration based on ΔI, which is computed as 11 12 -7 6 = -0.25. Since ΔI < 0, the change is confirmed and the temperature T is reduced with the cooling rate, i.e., T = 22.75 × 0.95 = 21.61.

The above procedures are repeated until the maximal intensity I( t′ H s , t′ H f ) of the new solution has been frozen and has stopped decreasing in the last few temperatures or the temperature has been reduced to zero. Samples of the configurations at different temperatures (with their corresponding probabilities) and the intensities of the different intervals (represented by the height of jobs belonging to them) are shown in Figure 3(b), (c), (d), and(e). Note that, since all of them have higher values of maximal intensities than the configuration in Figure 3(a), they can either be canceled or kept with rapidly decreasing probabilities with the reduction of temperature T . After some iterations, the state will eventually be frozen at the configurations similar to that in Figure 3(a) or Figure 3(f). It is not hard to see that all of them have the same value of maximal intensity and each one is schedulable. Note that for this particular example, the configuration converges quickly well before the temperature is reduced to zero.

Note that, when evaluating the configurations with regard to minimizing the overall energy consumption, although we can always use the total energy consumption as the metric for evaluation, we still prefer to use the intensity instead because it greatly reduces the time cost. Moreover, sometimes it is better to move back to a solution that was significantly better rather than always moving from the current state. This is called "restarting". Restarting is implemented by saving the best solution so far in S best and restarting the cooling schedule from there. The schedule could be restarted after a fixed number of steps, or when the current intensity is too high compared to the best solution so far.

div.head: VI. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, we use experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in scheduling task sets in real-time systems with (m, k)-constraints. Two groups of experiments were conducted to evaluate the corresponding schedulability guaranteeing capability and energy efficiency of different approaches for given task sets with (m, k)-constraints.

div.head: A. Comparison on schedulability guaranteeing capability
div.p: In the first group of experiments, we compare the performance of the different approaches in terms of providing prior off-line guarantee on the schedulability for randomly generated task sets. Specifically, we compared the performance of five different approaches. For the first approach App-E , the task sets are partitioned with the E-pattern from [3]. For the second approach App-E R , the task sets are partitioned with the E Rpattern from [9]. For the third approach App-R, the task sets are statically partitioned with the R-pattern from [13], which is also the pattern on which the approach in [22] is based in order to provide the prior off-line guarantee for its online algorithm. The fourth approach App-EE is our approach in Section IV which seeks to rotate the E-pattern adaptively to improve its schedulability. The fifth approach App-SA is our approach in Section V which adopts simulated annealing to determine the general appropriate regular (m, k)-pattern for any given task set. (We did not compare with the approaches in [7] because the approaches in [7] are based on computing the "interference" from higher priority tasks on lower priority tasks when fixed-priority scheduling is used, which are not applicable to systems scheduled under EDF scheduling policy.)

The periodic tasks sets were randomly generated with at least five tasks each. The periods were randomly chosen in the range of [10ms, 100ms] and the relative deadlines were randomly set to be less than or equal to the periods. The worst case execution time (WCET) was set to be uniformly distributed from 1 to its deadline. The m i and k i for the (m, k)-constraints were also randomly generated such that k i is uniformly distributed between 2 to 10, and m i < k i . Since it is proved in [9] that any task sets schedulable with Rpattern can be schedulable with any other (m, k)-pattern, we discarded those task sets schedulable with R-pattern as they do not provide any insight on the schedulability comparison between the different approaches. Consequently we also did not include the results for App-R in the evaluation for this group of comparison.

To reduce the statistical error, the (m/k)-utilization, i.e., ∑ i m i C i k i P i is divided into intervals of length 0.1 and within each interval, the task sets were randomly generated such that at least 100 task sets were schedulable by at least one of the approaches (except App-R) or at least 5000 task sets have been generated for the interval. Note that although we can always resort to simulation to check the schedulability of the task sets, some faster feasibility conditions can help greatly reduce the time consumption. In our experiment, for task sets to be scheduled with App-E, we check their schedulability with the feasibility condition in [9]. And for task sets with approaches App-E R , App-EE and App-SA, we check their schedulability based on Lemma 1. The numbers of task sets schedulable by each of the approaches are shown in Figure 4.

As seen from Figure 4, when the (m/k)-utilization is very low (e.g., less than 0.2), the schedulability of the different approaches are close to each other. However, as the (m/k)-utilization increases, the schedulability of App-E begins to degrade quickly. The schedulability of App-E R has marginal improvement over App-E but the is not very significant for most of the utilization intervals. With pattern adjustment based on rotation, App-EE can improve App-E significantly when the (m/k)-utilization is not too high or too low. The maximal improvement can be around 20%. However, as the (m/k)-utilization further increases, the improvement of App-EE over App-E also becomes limited. With more advanced pattern adjustment based on simulated annealing, App-SA can further improve over App-EE effectively and it always has the best performance among the different approaches. Moreover, the improvement becomes more significant as the (m/k)-utilization increases. For example, when the utilization is between [0.4,0.8], the average improvement of App-SA over App-E can be more than 34%. The experiment results also conform to our expectation that all task sets schedulable with App-E or App-E R are schedulable with App-EE and all task sets schedulable with the previous approaches are schedulable with App-SA.

div.head: B. Energy performance evaluation
div.p: In the second group of experiments, we test the performance of the different approaches in terms of energy consumption of the system. Note that for this group of experiments, we replaced the algorithm App-E R above with the energy conservation algorithm HYB E R in [9] which adopts a dynamic pattern based on the E R -pattern. We also implemented App-R with the energy constrained algorithm from [10] which is based on the R-pattern.

The processor model used in our experiments was the Intel XScale processor model [23] which we assumed to be able to run with available discrete speeds in the range of [0, 1 GHz] with step of 50MHz. According to [24], the power consumption function for Intel XScale [23] can be modeled approximately as P act (s) = 0.08 + 1.52s 3 Watts by treating 1GHz as the reference speed 1. The normalized critical speed in such a model is about 0.3 (at 297 MHz) with power consumption 0.12W. We assume the shut down overhead to be E o = 800µJ [24]. If the minimal processor speed is 0, the idle power consumption of the processor is 0.08 Watts and the corresponding shut down threshold will be T th = 10ms.

In this group of experiments, for the approaches based on a static pattern (i.e., App-R, App-E, App-EE, and App-SA ), we adopt the job level speed scaling because it can be closer to the lower bound of energy consumption with an ideally optimal voltage schedule. In doing that, the speed schedules of each task set within its hyperperiod are derived with Yao's algorithm [5] first. Then all job speeds less than the critical speed s crit are rounded up to s crit . For the approach based on a dynamic pattern (i.e., HYB E R ), since Yao's algorithm is not applicable any more, we just scale the speed of each task to be as low as the critical speed s crit at the task level with the feasibility condition in [9], and then during the runtime, the job speeds will be updated dynamically based on the approach in [9]. For all the approaches above, whenever a job speed is less than the critical speed s crit , it will be rounded up to s crit . Also for all approaches compared, the total energy consumption for each task set within twice of its hyperperiod will be computed with simulations.

The periodic task sets (including the periods, deadlines, WCETs, and m i and k i values) were randomly generated in the same way as in Section VI-A. We also divided the (m, k)utilization into intervals of length 0.1 and for each interval we randomly generated 50 feasible task sets. The energy consumption for each approach was collected and normalized to that of App-R, and the results are shown in Figure 5.

From Figure 5, the energy consumption of App-R is always the highest among the approaches based on static (m, k)patterns due to the poor schedulability of the R-pattern. Also when the utilization is very low, the energy consumption by the other approaches based on static (m, k)-patterns are close to each other because their levels of schedulability are similar, as shown in the first group of experiments. However, as the (m, k)-utilization increases, the energy consumption of App-EE becomes much better than App-E. The maximal energy reduction by App-EE over App-E can be around 25%. This is because, by rotating the E-pattern adaptively, App-EE is able to redistribute the mandatory workload of the whole task set more evenly within the hyperperiod. As a result, the intensities of the intervals can be effectively reduced. So the required speeds to execute the mandatory jobs within those intervals can also be lowered correspondingly. Furthermore, with our simulated annealing approach, the energy can be reduced even more significantly. For example, when the utilization is not high, the energy reduction achievable by App-SA over App-E can be nearly 32%. This is because, by adjusting the patterns in a more refined way with techniques based on simulated annealing, the patterns can be determined more flexibly and the intensities of the intervals can be further reduced effectively. As a result the required job speeds can be reduced much more effectively. This is especially true when the periods of the tasks are not co-prime with each other. It is also interesting to note that although the approach based on a dynamic pattern, i.e., HYB E R can reduce the dynamic energy efficiently as shown in [9], its performance is not so good when both dynamic and leakage energy are considered simultaneously. This is mainly because HYB E R optionally executed quite a few redundant jobs whose total energy cost cannot be compensated by the savings in dynamic energy alone. Another reason is that in general the job level speed schedule adopted by the approaches based on static patterns are closer to the lower bound of energy consumption required by the ideally optimal case and thus can be more energy efficient than the task level speed slowdown adopted by the approaches based on dynamic patterns.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this paper, we proposed two off-line approaches to improve the schedulability and energy efficiency for weakly hard real-time embedded systems. The first one intends to improve the previous evenly distributed (m, k)-pattern through adaptive pattern adjustment. The second one determines a more generalized regular (m, k)-pattern with techniques based on simulated annealing. Through extensive experiments, the results demonstrate that our proposed techniques outperform previous work significantly in both schedulability and energy efficiency for weakly hard real-time embedded systems.
